q: Which statement correctly defines electrolysis?
options: The production of an electric current from a chemical reaction between two different metals
The decomposition of any compound by heating it until it melts
The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current through it
The joining of two elements to form an ionic compound using an electric current
explain: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to break down an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water. The ions must be free to move.

q: In a simple electrolytic cell, which description of the anode is correct?
options: The negative electrode
The positive electrode
The molten or aqueous substance that is decomposed
The wire that joins the cell to the power supply
explain: The anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the power supply. The negative electrode is the cathode.

q: In electrolysis, which electrode is the cathode?
options: The positive electrode, which attracts positive ions
The negative electrode, which attracts negative ions
The negative electrode, which attracts positive ions
The positive electrode, where non-metals form
explain: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal, so it attracts positively charged ions (metal ions or hydrogen ions).

q: What is the electrolyte in an electrolysis experiment?
options: The solid rod that carries current into the cell
The battery or power supply that provides the current
The molten or aqueous substance that undergoes electrolysis
The gas given off at one of the electrodes
explain: The electrolyte is the liquid or solution containing mobile ions that is decomposed by the current.

q: Which sample cannot be electrolysed?
options: Molten sodium chloride
Molten lead(II) bromide
Solid sodium chloride
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate
explain: In a solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so no ions are free to carry charge. Molten or aqueous ionic compounds can be electrolysed.

q: Why does molten lead(II) bromide conduct electricity when solid lead(II) bromide does not?
options: The ions are formed only when the compound melts
Electrons are free to move when the compound melts
The ions are free to move when the compound is molten
The compound changes into a metal when it melts
explain: Solid ionic compounds have ions fixed in a lattice. When molten, the ions are mobile and carry the current.

q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Lead at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
explain: Lead is a metal so it forms at the negative cathode. Bromine is a non-metal so it forms at the positive anode.

q: Which observation is made at the anode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with graphite electrodes?
options: Red-brown fumes of bromine are seen
A silvery bead of molten lead forms
Colourless bubbles of hydrogen are seen
A pale green gas that bleaches litmus is seen
explain: Bromide ions lose electrons at the anode to form bromine, which is a red-brown vapour.

q: Which observation is made at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with graphite electrodes?
options: Red-brown fumes are given off
Colourless bubbles are given off
A pink-brown solid coats the electrode
A silver-grey bead of molten lead forms
explain: Lead ions gain electrons at the cathode to form lead metal, which is molten at the temperature of the experiment.

q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form at the cathode and anode?
options: Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
explain: Hydrogen ions from water are discharged at the cathode in preference to sodium ions. Chloride ions in concentrated solution are discharged at the anode as chlorine.

q: Which test and result show that a gas is chlorine?
options: A glowing splint relights
A lighted splint goes out with a squeaky pop
Limewater turns milky
Damp litmus paper is bleached
explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Relighting a glowing splint tests for oxygen, and a squeaky pop tests for hydrogen.

q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which test confirms the gas formed at the cathode?
options: A glowing splint relights
Damp litmus paper is bleached
A lighted splint burns with a squeaky pop
Limewater turns milky
explain: The gas at the cathode is hydrogen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which gas forms at the anode and how is it identified?
options: Oxygen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
Hydrogen, which relights a glowing splint
Oxygen, which relights a glowing splint
Sulfur dioxide, which bleaches damp litmus paper
explain: Oxygen is formed at the anode, and it relights a glowing splint.

q: Which row correctly shows the products of the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes?
options: oxygen | hydrogen
hydrogen | oxygen
hydrogen | sulfur dioxide
sulfur | oxygen
explain: Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, because water is effectively being decomposed.

q: Which statement about the products of electrolysis is correct?
options: Metals form at the anode, and non-metals form at the cathode
Metals or hydrogen form at the cathode, and non-metals other than hydrogen form at the anode
Hydrogen forms at the anode, and metals form at the cathode
Non-metals form at both electrodes
explain: Positive ions (metal ions or H⁺) move to the cathode and gain electrons. Negative ions (non-metal ions) move to the anode.

q: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Iodine at the cathode and potassium at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and iodine at the anode
Potassium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Potassium at the cathode and iodine at the anode
explain: A molten binary ionic compound gives the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.

q: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Chlorine at the cathode and zinc at the anode
Zinc at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Zinc at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
explain: Zn²⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and form zinc. Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and form chlorine.

q: Which compound gives a metal at the cathode and oxygen at the anode when it is electrolysed in the molten state?
options: Lead(II) oxide
Hydrogen chloride
Sodium chloride
Copper(II) bromide
explain: Lead(II) oxide contains Pb²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, so it forms lead and oxygen. The others contain chloride or bromide ions, or no metal.

q: Why are metal objects such as car bumpers electroplated?
options: To make them more dense and heavier
To make them conduct electricity better
To make them react more quickly with oxygen
To improve their appearance and resistance to corrosion
explain: Electroplating covers an object with a thin layer of a metal that looks attractive and protects the object underneath from corrosion.

q: A steel object is to be electroplated with nickel. How should the object be connected?
options: As the anode, in a solution containing nickel ions
As the cathode, in molten nickel(II) oxide
As the cathode, in a solution containing nickel ions
As the anode, in distilled water
explain: The object to be plated is the cathode so that positive nickel ions are attracted to it and gain electrons.

q: A steel spoon is to be silver-plated. Which row gives a correct set-up?
options: silver rod | spoon | silver nitrate solution
spoon | silver rod | silver nitrate solution
spoon | silver rod | sodium chloride solution
spoon | carbon rod | copper(II) sulfate solution
explain: The spoon is the cathode, the plating metal (silver) is the anode, and the electrolyte contains silver ions.

q: Why are graphite electrodes often used in electrolysis?
options: They dissolve easily so the electrolyte is replaced
They conduct electricity and do not react with most electrolytes
They are positive ions that move into the solution
They have a lower melting point than metals
explain: Graphite is inert and conducts electricity because of its delocalised electrons, so it carries current without taking part in the reaction.

q: A nickel layer is to be electroplated onto an iron fork. Which material should be used as the anode?
options: Iron
Graphite
Zinc
Nickel
explain: The anode is made of the plating metal, so nickel is used. Nickel dissolves and replaces the nickel ions removed at the cathode.

q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. How does the volume of hydrogen collected compare with the volume of oxygen?
options: The volume of hydrogen is half the volume of oxygen
The volumes are equal
The volume of hydrogen is four times the volume of oxygen
The volume of hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen
explain: Water is decomposed: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so two volumes of hydrogen form for each volume of oxygen.

q: Which electrolysis gives a metal at the cathode and a non-metal other than a halogen at the anode?
options: Molten sodium chloride
Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
Molten lead(II) oxide
Dilute sulfuric acid
explain: Molten lead(II) oxide gives lead and oxygen. Molten sodium chloride gives a halogen, and the two aqueous electrolytes give hydrogen at the cathode.

q: Which observations are made when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
options: Silvery metal at the cathode and pale green gas at the anode
Colourless gas at both electrodes
Red-brown fumes at the anode and silvery metal at the cathode
Colourless gas at the cathode and pale green gas at the anode
explain: Hydrogen (colourless) forms at the cathode and chlorine (pale green) forms at the anode.

q: As dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes for a long time, what happens to the acid solution?
options: It becomes more dilute because sulfate ions are used up
Its concentration stays the same because acid is only a catalyst
It turns into sulfur and hydrogen
It becomes more concentrated because water is used up
explain: Only water is decomposed to hydrogen and oxygen, so the same amount of acid is left in less water.

q: Which of these elements is formed at the anode during electrolysis?
options: Hydrogen
Bromine
Sodium
Copper
explain: Non-metals other than hydrogen form at the anode. Metals and hydrogen form at the cathode.

q: Two graphite rods dip into molten lead(II) bromide and are joined to a battery and a lamp. The lamp lights. What does this show?
options: Solid lead(II) bromide conducts electricity
Lead(II) bromide is a metal
Molten lead(II) bromide conducts electricity
Graphite rods dissolve in lead(II) bromide
explain: A lit lamp shows a complete circuit, so the molten ionic compound allows current to flow because its ions are mobile.

q: A key is copper-plated using a copper anode and copper(II) sulfate solution. What is seen at the key?
options: A pink-brown layer of copper forms on it
The key slowly dissolves
Bubbles of hydrogen form on it
A blue solid forms on it
explain: The key is the cathode, where Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons to form copper metal, a pink-brown solid.
